concepts.name: Structure and Tiers of Cooperative Banking in India
key_dimensions: Three-tier structure: State Cooperative Banks (SCBs), District Central Cooperative Banks (DCCBs), and Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS) — and the two-tier urban model
Distinction between rural cooperative banks and urban cooperative banks (UCBs) in terms of hierarchy and function
Role of NABARD vs RBI in supervising different tiers — a classic UPSC overlap trap
Why PACS are NOT regulated by RBI (not a 'bank' under Banking Regulation Act) — common exception tested

concepts.name: Dual Regulation of Cooperative Banks: RBI and State Registrar
key_dimensions: Banking operations regulated by RBI under Banking Regulation Act, 1949; incorporation/management governed by State Cooperative Societies Acts
The 'dual control' problem: how it leads to regulatory gaps and accountability issues
Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2020 — extension of RBI's powers over UCBs and multistate cooperative banks
Distinction: what RBI can and cannot control (e.g., RBI cannot supersede board of a cooperative bank the same way it can for commercial banks — key trap)

concepts.name: Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2020 and Its Impact on Cooperative Banks
key_dimensions: Key changes: audit, capital requirement norms, and RBI's power to initiate amalgamation/reconstruction without moratorium
Extension of Sections 45-IE (supersession of board) provisions — how cooperative banks are still treated differently from SCBs
PACS and primary cooperative societies doing non-banking business explicitly excluded from purview
Context: PMC Bank crisis as the trigger for the amendment — UPSC loves policy-crisis linkages

concepts.name: Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS): Role, Regulation, and Computerisation
key_dimensions: PACS as the grassroots unit of short-term rural cooperative credit — not regulated by RBI or NABARD directly
Regulated under respective State Cooperative Societies Act — no uniform national law
Government scheme for computerisation of 63,000 PACS (approved 2022) — linkage to DBT, common accounting system
PACS vs Kisan Credit Card (KCC) delivery mechanism — how PACS serve as last-mile for agricultural credit

concepts.name: NABARD's Supervisory Role over Rural Cooperative Banks
key_dimensions: NABARD conducts inspection of State Cooperative Banks and DCCBs under Section 35(6) of Banking Regulation Act — on behalf of RBI
NABARD's refinancing role vs its supervisory/inspection role — conceptual distinction
NABARD's role in capital assistance and revival packages for weak cooperative banks (e.g., STCCS recapitalisation)
Overlap trap: NABARD supervises SCBs and DCCBs; RBI directly supervises Urban Cooperative Banks

concepts.name: Urban Cooperative Banks (UCBs): Classification, Regulation, and Vulnerabilities
key_dimensions: Categorisation into Tier 1, 2, 3, 4 based on deposit size (RBI's 2022 revised framework) — specific thresholds tested
Voluntary transition of UCBs to Small Finance Banks — RBI's on-tap licensing route and eligibility criteria
Key vulnerabilities: connected lending, governance failures, lack of professional management
PMC Bank, Madhavpura Mercantile Cooperative Bank — case studies of failure and regulatory response

concepts.name: Short-Term Cooperative Credit Structure (STCCS) vs Long-Term Cooperative Credit Structure (LTCCS)
key_dimensions: STCCS: three-tier (SCB–DCCB–PACS) for crop loans and working capital; LTCCS: two-tier (State Cooperative Agriculture and Rural Development Banks–Primary Cooperative Agriculture and Rural Development Banks) for investment credit
LTCCS refinanced by NABARD; direct lending to farmers for land development, farm mechanisation
Decline and merger of LTCCS institutions — policy shift towards direct bank lending
Vaidyanathan Committee recommendations on STCCS revival — conditions attached to recapitalisation

concepts.name: Deposit Insurance Coverage for Cooperative Banks
key_dimensions: DICGC (Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation) covers deposits in cooperative banks including UCBs — ₹5 lakh limit
PACS NOT covered under DICGC — because they are not licensed banks under Banking Regulation Act
DICGC Amendment Act, 2021: timeline-based insurance payment even during moratorium (90-day rule) — triggered by PMC Bank issue
Common trap: whether all cooperative banks are covered — answer is licensed cooperative banks only

concepts.name: Vaidyanathan Committee Recommendations on Cooperative Credit Institutions
key_dimensions: Two committees (2004 and 2006): revival of STCCS and LTCCS respectively
Conditional recapitalisation: states required to sign MoU, pass legislative amendments (remove state government's power to supersede boards)
Recommendations on governance: one member-one vote vs proportional voting; professionalisation of management
Implementation status: partial adoption — UPSC often tests what was recommended vs what was implemented

concepts.name: Multistate Cooperative Societies Act, 2002 and Its Banking Implications
key_dimensions: Multistate cooperative banks registered under MSCS Act, 2002 — regulated by Central Registrar, not state registrar
RBI's banking regulation applies; but management/membership governed by MSCS Act
Multistate Cooperative Societies (Amendment) Act, 2023 — key changes: concurrent audit, Cooperative Election Authority, dispute resolution
Trap: multistate cooperative banks vs national cooperative banks — understanding jurisdictional hierarchy

concepts.name: Conversion of Cooperative Banks to Small Finance Banks (SFBs)
key_dimensions: RBI's 2018 on-tap SFB licensing guidelines allow voluntary conversion of UCBs meeting eligibility criteria
Conditions: minimum net worth ₹100 crore, satisfactory track record, shareholder consent mechanism challenge
Challenge: cooperative structure (one member-one vote) vs company structure (shareholding-based) — conversion requires dissolution of cooperative society
Examples: Shivalik Mercantile Cooperative Bank — first UCB to convert to SFB (2021)

concepts.name: Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (PMJDY) and Cooperative Banks' Role
key_dimensions: Cooperative banks included as Business Correspondents under financial inclusion framework — but limited compared to commercial banks
Cooperative banks' restricted ability to expand branches due to dual regulation (state government approval needed in addition to RBI)
Urban cooperative banks' role in serving lower-middle income urban segments — niche not addressed by commercial banks
Comparison trap: why cooperative banks are less effective than SFBs or RRBs in financial inclusion delivery

concepts.name: Capital Adequacy and Prudential Norms for Cooperative Banks
key_dimensions: RBI introduced CRAR (Capital to Risk-weighted Assets Ratio) norms for UCBs — 9% minimum; phased implementation for rural cooperative banks
Rural cooperative banks (SCBs, DCCBs) follow different, less stringent prudential norms compared to UCBs
Challenge of raising capital in cooperative structure: cannot issue equity shares to public; limited to shares to members
Post-2020 amendment: RBI can allow UCBs to issue equity shares or preference shares to members or others with prior approval

concepts.name: Cooperative Banks and Priority Sector Lending (PSL) Obligations
key_dimensions: UCBs: PSL target is 40% of adjusted net bank credit (ANBC) — similar to commercial banks; rural cooperative banks have different norms
Within PSL, agricultural sub-targets and weaker section targets applicable to UCBs — specific percentages tested
Cooperative banks as primary conduit for agricultural credit — overlap with NABARD's role in channelling funds
Recent policy push: increasing formal credit to agriculture through PACS-KCC linkage under PSL framework

concepts.name: Governance Issues and Board Composition in Cooperative Banks
key_dimensions: Democratic governance principle (one member-one vote) vs need for professional management — inherent tension
RBI's 'fit and proper' criteria for directors of UCBs (post-2020 amendment) — professionals on board mandatory
Political interference: state government nominees on boards of SCBs and DCCBs — conflict with RBI's autonomy goals
Expert Committee on Urban Cooperative Banks (N.S. Vishwanathan Committee, 2019) — recommendations on umbrella organisation

concepts.name: Umbrella Organisation for Cooperative Banks
key_dimensions: Concept: a National Umbrella Organisation (NUO) to provide liquidity support, IT infrastructure, and training to cooperative banks
RBI in-principle approval for National Cooperative Finance and Development Corporation (NCFDC) as umbrella body for UCBs
Distinction: NUO for UCBs vs NABARD's role for rural cooperatives — different umbrella structures
Rationale: cooperative banks too small individually to afford core banking solutions, cyber security infrastructure

concepts.name: Non-Performing Assets (NPAs) and Financial Health of Cooperative Banks
key_dimensions: Cooperative banks historically have higher NPA ratios compared to SCBs — reasons: political lending, weak recovery mechanisms
State Cooperative Banks and DCCBs: NPA provisioning norms less stringent than commercial banks — UPSC trap on differential regulation
Recovery mechanisms: Cooperative banks cannot use SARFAESI Act 2002 directly — amendment in 2013 extended SARFAESI to cooperative banks with asset size above ₹1 lakh
SARFAESI applicability trap: applies only to cooperative banks registered under state/central acts AND having ₹1 lakh+ loan outstanding — conditions matter

concepts.name: Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) vs Cooperative Banks: Key Distinctions
key_dimensions: RRBs are statutory bodies under RRB Act 1976 — scheduled commercial banks; cooperative banks are registered under cooperative society laws — different legal status
Ownership: RRBs have tripartite ownership (Centre 50%, State 15%, Sponsor bank 35%); cooperative banks owned by members
Regulation: RRBs solely regulated by RBI/NABARD; cooperative banks face dual regulation
UPSC trap: both serve rural credit needs — but RRBs are NOT cooperative banks and have different PSL obligations, CRAR norms, and governance structure

concepts.name: Constitutional Provisions and Cooperative Societies: 97th Constitutional Amendment
key_dimensions: 97th Amendment (2011): added Article 19(1)(c) right to form cooperative societies; inserted Part IXB (Articles 243ZH to 243ZT) for cooperative societies
Part IXB: provisions for democratic elections, term of office (5 years), reservation for SC/ST and women on boards

Supreme Court in Rajendra N. Shah v. Union of India (2021): Part IXB struck down partially — Parliament cannot legislate on state cooperative societies (federal issue); only applicable to multistate cooperative societies
Cooperative banking trap: 97th Amendment applies to cooperative societies broadly, but cooperative BANKS additionally governed by Banking Regulation Act — dual constitutional-regulatory framework

concepts.name: Kisan Credit Card (KCC) Scheme and Cooperative Banks
key_dimensions: KCC introduced in 1998 — cooperative banks, RRBs, and commercial banks are all delivery channels
Cooperative banks (especially PACS-linked) are the primary KCC issuers in states like Maharashtra, Gujarat
Modified KCC (2012): includes allied activities, post-harvest expenses, consumption needs — expanded scope
Challenge: cooperative banks' technology gap limits real-time KCC operations; PACS computerisation scheme aims to bridge this gap — policy linkage
